name: Forces on Current-Carrying Conductors
what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by a current-carrying wire placed in an external magnetic field. It includes using the right-hand slap rule to find force direction and applying the formula F = nIlB to calculate force magnitude.
why: The force on a current-carrying conductor is the mechanism by which electrical energy is converted to mechanical energy in motors, speakers, and many other devices. Mastering this section is essential for analysing DC motors.

items.title: I can explain why a current-carrying wire in an external magnetic field experiences a force
items.what: A current-carrying wire has its own magnetic field. When placed in an external magnetic field, these two fields interact to produce a net force on the wire. By Newton's third law, the wire exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet.
items.why: This effect is the reverse of Ørsted's discovery: just as current produces a field, a field acts on a current. Understanding both directions of this relationship is necessary for analysing motors and generators.
items.example: A wire carrying current horizontally between the poles of a horseshoe magnet will be pushed upward or downward depending on the current direction. Reversing the current reverses the force direction.

items.title: I can use the right-hand slap rule to determine the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
items.what: Hold your right hand flat. Point your thumb in the direction of conventional current and your outstretched fingers in the direction of the magnetic field. Your palm pushes in the direction of the force on the wire.
items.why: The force direction depends on both the current direction and the field direction in a three-dimensional way that is hard to reason through without a systematic rule. The right-hand slap rule gives a reliable, repeatable method.
items.example: For a wire carrying current to the right in a field directed into the page: thumb points right, fingers point into the page, palm faces upward — so the force on the wire is directed upward (toward the top of the page).

items.title: I can calculate the force on a current-carrying conductor using F = nIlB
items.what: The magnetic force on a conductor is given by F = nIlB, where n is the number of wires, I is the current in amperes, l is the length of wire in metres, and B is the magnetic field strength in tesla. This applies when the current is perpendicular to the field.
items.why: This formula quantifies how increasing current, field strength, wire length, or number of wires each proportionally increases the force. It is used to design motors, calculate torques, and solve exam problems.
items.example: A single wire (n = 1) of length 0.40 m carrying a current of 0.50 A in a field of 0.20 T perpendicular to the wire experiences a force of F = 1 × 0.50 × 0.40 × 0.20 = 0.040 N.

items.title: I can explain why no magnetic force acts on a wire when it is parallel to the magnetic field
items.what: When the current direction is parallel (or anti-parallel) to the magnetic field, no force is produced. A magnetic force only results when the current and field are perpendicular to each other.
items.why: This is a common source of errors in calculations. Recognising when the angle between current and field is zero (parallel) tells you immediately that the force is zero, with no calculation needed.
items.example: A wire carrying current toward the north in a magnetic field also directed toward the north experiences zero force. Rotating the wire to run east-west (perpendicular to the northward field) would produce the maximum force.
